newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: France's Chirac sees bright EU-Latin America future.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac sees bright EU-Latin America future.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac said on Tuesday the Americas were too small for South America's Mercosur customs union and the fast-growing group was bound to develop a partnership with the European Union.

Chirac, winding up a tour of Mercosur countries Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, plus Bolivia, said the pace of the group's growth would force it to look across the Atlantic, beyond the all-America free trade area proposed for 2005.
He said the five countries had warmly welcomed his proposal for an EU-Latin American summit next year to set up an economic, political and education partnership and build on a 1995 accord.

"We must give life to this accord, give it its full scope," he told the Argentine congress, noting that the EU is already Mercosur's main trade partner, ahead of the North American free trade bloc (NAFTA) grouping Canada, Mexico and the United States.
A quarter of Mercosur's exports were going to the EU, compared with 17 percent to NAFTA. More than half the EU's exports to Latin America were going to Mercosur, Chirac said.

He acknowledged demands from Brazil and Argentina, the two largest Mercosur economies, to ease EU trade barriers to their farm exports. "We will have to achieve complete liberalisation of our exchanges. This will obviously involve fierce negotiations, particularly on farm products," he said.
He has previously dismissed charges of EU protectionism, saying Mercosur's farm exports to the EU exceeded by six times its European farm imports.
Argentine President Carlos Menem has also complained about France's large bilateral trade surplus and French officials said Chirac promised to work towards correcting the imbalance.

Chirac said France and Argentina, its closest partner in the region, must be the driving forces in boosting cooperation between Latin America and Europe. He said he would personally oversee the follow-up to his trip to ensure concrete results and would visit all other Latin American countries next year.

Chirac also appeared to bury a long-standing dispute over the kidnapping of two French nuns by former navy Capt. Alfredo Astiz during the military's "dirty war" on leftists in the 1970s. "I deeply regret that this murderer has not been punished," he said, but he could not go against Argentina's amnesty for the military.
France has an international arrest warrant out for Astiz, who retired from the navy last year.
In a symbolical gesture, Chirac gave Menem a flag French troops seized from Argentines at the battle of Vuelta de Obligado in 1845, the only time the two countries ever fought each other.
"Let this flag be the symbol of our common ambition, of the fresh impulse the Argentine and French people want to give their exceptional nearly two-century-old friendship," he said.
Chirac was flying home later in the day.
